newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.N.'s Ogata says Zaire worst refugee crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.N.'s Ogata says Zaire worst refugee crisis.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s refugee agency on Tuesday slammed the international community over the crisis in Zaire and said the refugee situation there was the worst her agency had faced.

U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata told a news conference in Cape Town, where she met President Nelson Mandela on Monday, that her staff had been abandoned by the international community.
"It is the most worrying and difficult operation that I think our office has really gone through and (with) a lot of sacrifice of human life -- that's what's at stake," she said.
"(We have been abandoned) by the international community or by governments...Neglect, reluctance, it's a reality," she said.
Ogata said the international community could have acted earlier to separate soldiers responsible for massacres in Burundi and Rwanda from innocent civilian refugees.
"The reluctance of dispatching military is very serious. I feel that very strongly.

"Had we had some kind of military capacity to help humanitarian activities, we would not be left where we are today: Looking for refugees for the last three months and finally finding them right in the middle of the conflict."

The UNHCR says there are nearly 400,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees still dotted around Zaire. This figure is challenged as too high by some countries, notably those opposed to any foreign intervention in Zaire.
In a speech to South African legislators earlier, she said the crisis in Zaire was partly a result of the failure of the international community to intervene.

"The absence of a convergence of interests and views among the major powers also results in preventing this drama from receiving the international attention and determination it deserves for solution," she said.

Analysts said she was referring to reported tension between the United States and France over the diplomatic spoils in Central Africa, a tussle some have blamed for the lack of pressure to end the fighting in which rebels have seized about a quarter of Zaire.
Ogata repeated her criticism at the news conference later, saying she was dismayed that a military force proposed for Central Africa last year had not been formed.

She said it was too late for multinational intervention in Zaire but urged African nations to combine forces to establish a quick-reaction unit to intervene in new conflicts before they escalate too far.

Mandela last year rejected a U.S. proposal for an African crisis-intervention force that would be trained, armed and partly financed by the major powers. "That initiative must come from Africa," he had said.
Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said at Ogata's news conference, however, that South Africa had accepted the need to contribute troops to an African peacekeeping force.
He added that many of the reservations expressed when the United States made the proposal last year had been addressed.
